blocks.text: The firemen’s forecastle of a transatlantic liner an hour after sailing from New York for the voyage across. Tiers of narrow, steel bunks, three deep, on all sides. An entrance in rear. Benches on the floor before the bunks. The room is crowded with men, shouting, cursing, laughing, singing﻿—a confused, inchoate uproar swelling into a sort of unity, a meaning﻿—the bewildered, furious, baffled defiance of a beast in a cage. Nearly all the men are drunk. Many bottles are passed from hand to hand. All are dressed in dungaree pants, heavy ugly shoes. Some wear singlets, but the majority are stripped to the waist.

The treatment of this scene, or of any other scene in the play, should by no means be naturalistic. The effect sought after is a cramped space in the bowels of a ship, imprisoned by white steel. The lines of bunks, the uprights supporting them, cross each other like the steel framework of a cage. The ceiling crushes down upon the men’s heads. They cannot stand upright. This accentuates the natural stooping posture which shovelling coal and the resultant over-development of back and shoulder muscles have given them. The men themselves should resemble those pictures in which the appearance of Neanderthal Man is guessed at. All are hairy-chested, with long arms of tremendous power, and low, receding brows above their small, fierce, resentful eyes. All the civilized white races are represented, but except for the slight differentiation in color of hair, skin, eyes, all these men are alike.
Drunk as a lord, God stiffen you!
Pass back that bottle, damn you!
Ho, Froggy! Where the devil have you been?
I hit him smash in yaw, py Gott!
And the coppers nabbed him﻿—and I run﻿—
I like peer better. It don’t pig head gif you.
A slut, I’m sayin’! She robbed me aslape﻿—
Commotion. Two men about to fight are pulled apart.
He packa da wallop, I tella you!
No fightin’, maties. We’re all chums, ain’t we?
A voice starts bawling a song.
“Beer, beer, glorious beer! Fill yourselves right up to here.”
For the first time seeming to take notice of the uproar about him, turns around threateningly﻿—in a tone of contemptuous authority.

Several bottles are eagerly offered. He takes a tremendous gulp at one of them; then, keeping the bottle in his hand, glares belligerently at the owner, who hastens to acquiesce in this robbery by saying:
We must be passing the Hook.
She’s beginning to roll to it.
Six days in hell﻿—and then Southampton.
Py Yesus, I vish somepody take my first vatch for me!
Absinthe? It’s doped. You’ll go off your chump, Froggy!
Sing us that whiskey song, Paddy.
They all turn to an old, wizened Irishman who is dozing, very drunk, on the benches forward. His face is extremely monkey-like with all the sad, patient pathos of that animal in his small eyes.
He’s gettin’ old. The drink is too much for him.

Blinking about him, starts to his feet resentfully, swaying, holding on to the edge of a bunk. I’m never too drunk to sing. ’Tis only when I’m dead to the world I’d be wishful to sing at all. With a sort of sad contempt. “Whiskey Johnny,” ye want? A chanty, ye want? Now that’s a queer wish from the ugly like of you, God help you. But no matther. He starts to sing in a thin, nasal, doleful tone:

Oh, whiskey is the life of man! Whiskey! O Johnny! They all join in on this. Oh, whiskey is the life of man! Whiskey for my Johnny! Again chorus. Oh, whiskey drove my old man mad! Whiskey! O Johnny! Oh, whiskey drove my old man mad! Whiskey for my Johnny!
Repeating the word after him as one with same cynical amused mockery.
The chorused word has a brazen metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a general uproar of hard, barking laughter.
Don’t be cracking your head wid ut, Yank.
A whole chorus of voices has taken up this refrain, stamping on the floor, pounding on the benches with fists.
Taking a gulp from his bottle﻿—good-naturedly.
The uproar subsides. A very drunken sentimental tenor begins to sing:
“Far away in Canada, Far across the sea, There’s a lass who fondly waits Making a home for me﻿—”
In a more placated but still contemptuous tone.
Very drunk, jumps on a bench excitedly, gesticulating with a bottle in his hand.
There had been a gradual murmur of contemptuous resentment rising among the men until now he is interrupted by a storm of catcalls, hisses, boos, hard laughter.
With a great hard pride in them.
He never could hold up his end.
Yank’s right. We make it go.
Py Gott, Yank say right ting!
We don’t need noone cryin’ over us.
I’ll break his jaw for him!
Who has been sitting in a blinking, melancholy daze﻿—suddenly cries out in a voice full of old sorrow.
His voice runs into the wail of a keen, he rocks back and forth on his bench. The men stare at him, startled and impressed in spite of themselves.
With a sort of religious exaltation.
His tone of exaltation ceases. He goes on mournfully.
Who has been listening with a contemptuous sneer, barks out the answer.
As if to himself﻿—with great sorrow.
He suddenly bursts forth vehemently, growing more and more excited.
Is heard now﻿—throws his head back with a mocking burst of laughter.
Drawing back his fist, with a snarl.
“I care for nobody, no, not I, And nobody cares for me.”

Two days out. A section of the promenade deck. Mildred Douglas and her aunt are discovered reclining in deck chairs. The former is a girl of twenty, slender, delicate, with a pale, pretty face marred by a self-conscious expression of disdainful superiority. She looks fretful, nervous and discontented, bored by her own anemia. Her aunt is a pompous and proud﻿—and fat﻿—old lady. She is a type even to the point of a double chin and lorgnettes. She is dressed pretentiously, as if afraid her face alone would never indicate her position in life. Mildred is dressed all in white.

The impression to be conveyed by this scene is one of the beautiful, vivid life of the sea all about﻿—sunshine on the deck in a great flood, the fresh sea wind blowing across it. In the midst of this, these two incongruous, artificial figures, inert and disharmonious, the elder like a gray lump of dough touched up with rouge, the younger looking as if the vitality of her stock had been sapped before she was conceived, so that she is the expression not of its life energy but merely of the artificialities that energy had won for itself in the spending.
My great-grandmother smoked a pipe﻿—a clay pipe.
She was too distant a relative to be vulgar. Time mellows pipes.
Going on as if she hadn’t heard.
Protesting with a trace of genuine earnestness.
I don’t know what you are talking about.
She looks at her wrist watch.
Grandfather started as a puddler. I should have inherited an immunity to heat that would make a salamander shiver. It will be fun to put it to the test.
But don’t you have to have the captain’s﻿—or someone’s﻿—permission to visit the stokehole?
Throwing off her rugs and getting to her feet.
In just a second, ma’am. I’m waiting for the Fourth. He’s coming along.
Disturbed by her eyes, glances out to sea﻿—blurts out.
But it’s hot enough in the sun﻿—
Not hot enough for me. I don’t like Nature. I was never athletic.
My grandfather was a puddler. He played with boiling steel.
You’ll likely rub against oil and dirt. It can’t be helped.
It doesn’t matter. I have lots of white dresses.
I have an old coat you might throw over﻿—
I have fifty dresses like this. I will throw this one into the sea when I come back. That ought to wash it clean, don’t you think?
I will wear this very dress and none other.
No offence meant. It’s none of my business. I was only warning you﻿—
Looking down the deck﻿—with a sigh of relief.
Take care. He said there were dark alleyways﻿—
Yes, for a fresh pose I have no doubt you would drag the name of Douglas in the gutter!
From which it sprang. Goodbye, Aunt. Don’t pray too hard that I may fall into the fiery furnace.
She slaps her aunt insultingly across the face and walks off, laughing gaily.

The stokehole. In the rear, the dimly-outlined bulks of the furnaces and boilers. High overhead one hanging electric bulb sheds just enough light through the murky air laden with coal dust to pile up masses of shadows everywhere. A line of men, stripped to the waist, is before the furnace doors. They bend over, looking neither to right nor left, handling their shovels as if they were part of their bodies, with a strange, awkward, swinging rhythm. They use the shovels to throw open the furnace doors. Then from these fiery round holes in the black a flood of terrific light and heat pours full upon the men who are outlined in silhouette in the crouching, inhuman attitudes of chained gorillas. The men shovel with a rhythmic motion, swinging as on a pivot from the coal which lies in heaps on the floor behind to hurl it into the flaming mouths before them. There is a tumult of noise﻿—the brazen clang of the furnace doors as they are flung open or slammed shut, the grating, teeth-gritting grind of steel against steel, of crunching coal. This clash of sounds stuns one’s ears with its rending dissonance. But there is order in it, rhythm, a mechanical regulated recurrence, a tempo. And rising above all, making the air hum with the quiver of liberated energy, the roar of leaping flames in the furnaces, the monotonous throbbing beat of the engines.

As the curtain rises, the furnace doors are shut. The men are taking a breathing spell. One or two are arranging the coal behind them, pulling it into more accessible heaps. The others can be dimly made out leaning on their shovels in relaxed attitudes of exhaustion.
From the center of the line﻿—with exuberant scorn.
In an exultant tone of command.

At this last all the men, who have followed his movements of getting into position, throw open their furnace doors with a deafening clang. The fiery light floods over their shoulders as they bend round for the coal. Rivulets of sooty sweat have traced maps on their backs. The enlarged muscles form bunches of high light and shadow.
Chanting a count as he shovels without seeming effort.
His voice rising exultantly in the joy of battle.

This last in the chanting formula of the gallery gods at the six-day bike race. He slams his furnace door shut. The others do likewise with as much unison as their wearied bodies will permit. The effect is of one fiery eye after another being blotted out with a series of accompanying bangs.
There is a pause. Then the inexorable whistle sounds again from the dim regions above the electric light. There is a growl of cursing rage from all sides.

And hurls his shovel after them at the door which has just closed. It hits the steel bulkhead with a clang and falls clattering on the steel floor. From overhead the whistle sounds again in a long, angry, insistent command.
Py golly, a fallar gat gat grub in him.
Yank feeda da fire, no feeda da face.
Hey, Yank, you forgot to wash.
Give yer the bleedin’ itch, that’s wot.
It makes spots on you﻿—like a leopard.
Like a piebald nigger, you mean.
Repeating the word after him as one with cynical mockery.
The word has a brazen, metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a chorus of hard, barking laughter.
Springing to his feet and glaring at them belligerently.
With a wink at the others.
Repeating the word after him as one with cynical mockery.
The word has a brazen, metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a chorus of hard, barking laughter.
With a bitter, ironical scorn, increasing as he goes on.
A growl of anger goes up from all sides.
There is a roar of rage from all sides.

Straight as string! The bleedin’ steward as waits on ’em, ’e told me about ’er. And what’re we goin’ ter do, I arsks yer? ’Ave we got ter swaller ’er hinsults like dogs? It ain’t in the ship’s articles. I tell yer we got a case. We kin go ter law﻿—
Repeating the word after him as one with cynical mockery.
The word has a brazen metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a chorus of hard, barking laughter.
Feeling the ground slipping from under his feet﻿—desperately.
Repeating the word after him as one with cynical mockery.
The word has a brazen metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a chorus of hard, barking laughter.
Repeating the word after him as one with cynical mockery.
The word has a brazen metallic quality as if their throats were phonograph horns. It is followed by a chorus of hard, barking laughter.
Long slinks back out of sight.
Continuing the trend of his thoughts as if he had never been interrupted﻿—bitterly.
And there was Yank roarin’ curses and turning round wid his shovel to brain her﻿—and she looked at him, and him at her﻿—
A grin breaking over his face.
There is a roar of laughter from all.
With a grotesque imitation of a woman’s voice.
Divil a bit! Ain’t I wishin’ myself you’d brained her?
She looked it at you if she didn’t say the word itself.
Bursting into rage﻿—as if she were still in front of him.
Turning to the others, bewilderment seizing him again.
And be ’anged for murder or ’lectrocuted? She ain’t bleedin’ well worth it.

I don’t give a damn what! I’d be square wit her, wouldn’t I? Tink I wanter let her put somep’n over on me? Tink I’m goin’ to let her git away wit dat stuff? Yuh don’t know me! Noone ain’t never put nothin’ over on me and got away wit it, see!﻿—not dat kind of stuff﻿—no guy and no skoit neither! I’ll fix her! Maybe she’ll come down again﻿—
No chance, Yank. You scared her out of a year’s growth.
He extends his right arm, swelling out the great muscles.
She’ll never come. She’s had her belly-full, I’m telling you. She’ll be in bed now, I’m thinking, wid ten doctors and nurses feedin’ her salts to clean the fear out of her.
Shaking one fist upward and beating on his chest with the other.
He makes a rush for the door.
They have all piled on him and, after a fierce struggle, by sheer weight of numbers have borne him to the floor just inside the door.
Frenziedly, from the bottom of the heap.

Three weeks later. A corner of Fifth Avenue in the Fifties on a fine, Sunday morning. A general atmosphere of clean, well-tidied, wide street; a flood of mellow, tempered sunshine; gentle, genteel breezes. In the rear, the show windows of two shops, a jewelry establishment on the corner, a furrier’s next to it. Here the adornments of extreme wealth are tantalizingly displayed. The jeweler’s window is gaudy with glittering diamonds, emeralds, rubies, pearls, etc., fashioned in ornate tiaras, crowns, necklaces, collars, etc. From each piece hangs an enormous tag from which a dollar sign and numerals in intermittent electric lights wink out the incredible prices. The same in the furrier’s. Rich furs of all varieties hang there bathed in a downpour of artificial light. The general effect is of a background of magnificence cheapened and made grotesque by commercialism, a background in tawdry disharmony with the clear light and sunshine on the street itself.
Indicating it all with an oratorical gesture.
Looking up and down the avenue﻿—surlily.
In church, blarst ’em! Arskin’ Jesus to give ’em more money.
With a grin and a swagger.
Did yer old man follow the sea?
Not bad? Well, we pays for it wiv our bloody sweat, if yer wants to know!
Wait and yer’ll bloody well see﻿—
I don’t wait for noone. I keep on de move. Say, what yuh drag me up here for, anyway? Tryin’ to kid me, yuh simp, yuh?
Yer wants to get back at her, don’t yer? That’s what yer been saying’ every bloomin’ ’our since she hinsulted yer.
As disgusted as he dares to be.
He turns and sees the window display in the two stores for the first time.
With a gesture of sweeping the jewelers into oblivion.
Who has moved to the furriers﻿—indignantly.
Who has been staring at something inside﻿—with queer excitement.
Clenching his fists, his face growing pale with rage as if the skin in the window were a personal insult.
Dear Doctor Caiaphas! He is so sincere!
What was the sermon? I dozed off.
About the radicals, my dear﻿—and the false doctrines that are being preached.
We must organize a hundred percent American bazaar.
And let everyone contribute one one-hundredth percent of their income tax.
We can devote the proceeds to rehabilitating the veil of the temple.
But that has been done so many times.
Glaring from one to the other of them﻿—with an insulting snort of scorn.
Without seeming to see him, they make wide detours to avoid the spot where he stands in the middle of the sidewalk.
He swaggers away and deliberately lurches into a top-hatted gentleman, then glares at him pugnaciously.
Savagely﻿—giving him a push that sends him sprawling.
He approaches a lady﻿—with a vicious grin and a smirking wink.
Pointing to a skyscraper across the street which is in process of construction﻿—with bravado.
But as they seem neither to see nor hear him, he flies into a fury.
He turns in a rage on the men, bumping viciously into them but not jarring them the least bit. Rather it is he who recoils after each collision. He keeps growling.
But, without seeming to see him, they all answer with mechanical affected politeness:
Then at a cry from one of the women, they all scurry to the furrier’s window.
Ecstatically, with a gasp of delight.
The whole crowd of men and women chorus after her in the same tone of affected delight.
With a jerk of his head back on his shoulders, as if he had received a punch full in the face﻿—raging.
Seeing a fight﻿—with a roar of joy as he springs to his feet.
He lets drive a terrific swing, his fist landing full on the fat gentleman’s face. But the gentleman stands unmoved as if nothing had happened.
He claps his hands and begins to scream:

Night of the following day. A row of cells in the prison on Blackwells Island. The cells extend back diagonally from right front to left rear. They do not stop, but disappear in the dark background as if they ran on, numberless, into infinity. One electric bulb from the low ceiling of the narrow corridor sheds its light through the heavy steel bars of the cell at the extreme front and reveals part of the interior. Yank can be seen within, crouched on the edge of his cot in the attitude of Rodin’s The Thinker. His face is spotted with black and blue bruises. A bloodstained bandage is wrapped around his head.
Suddenly starting as if awakening from a dream, reaches out and shakes the bars﻿—aloud to himself, wonderingly.
A burst of hard, barking laughter comes from the unseen occupants of the cells, runs back down the tier, and abruptly ceases.
Steel, eh? You said a mouthful. This is the old iron house.
He’s the bloke they brung in out of his head. The bulls had beat him up fierce.
Say, guy! Who are you? No, never mind lying. What are you?
Yes, tell us your sad story. What’s your game?
What did they jug yuh for?
Then with sudden rage, rattling his cell bars.
Huh! You’re a hard boiled duck ain’t you!
Aw, can it. He’s a regular guy. Ain’t you?
What did he say he was﻿—a ape?
A silence. Then a furious rattling of bars from down the corridor.
You’ll have the guard down on us!
Angry exclamations from all the cells.
Did yuh beat up de odder guy?
Let him rave. It’s fun listenin’.
He rattles the bars of his cell furiously.
Take her for all she’s got!
What was this dame, anyway? Who was she, eh?
I dunno. First cabin stiff. Her old man’s a millionaire, dey says﻿—name of Douglas.
Douglas? That’s the president of the Steel Trust, I bet.
Sure. I seen his mug in de papers.
Hey, feller, take a tip from me. If you want to get back at that dame, you better join the Wobblies. You’ll get some action then.
A perfect storm of hisses, catcalls, boos, and hard laughter.
A terrific chorus of barking and yapping.
Sure. Give it to him. On’y keep it to yourself, see. We don’t wanter listen to no more of that slop.
Here you are. Hide it under your mattress.
He shakes the bars of his cell door till the whole tier trembles. Irritated, protesting exclamations from those awakened or trying to get to sleep.

Nearly a month later. An I.W.W. local near the waterfront, showing the interior of a front room on the ground floor, and the street outside. Moonlight on the narrow street, buildings massed in black shadow. The interior of the room, which is general assembly room, office, and reading room, resembles some dingy settlement boys club. A desk and high stool are in one corner. A table with papers, stacks of pamphlets, chairs about it, is at center. The whole is decidedly cheap, banal, commonplace and unmysterious as a room could well be. The secretary is perched on the stool making entries in a large ledger. An eye shade casts his face into shadows. Eight or ten men, longshoremen, iron workers, and the like, are grouped about the table. Two are playing checkers. One is writing a letter. Most of them are smoking pipes. A big signboard is on the wall at the rear, “Industrial Workers of the World﻿—Local No. 57.”

Comes down the street outside. He is dressed as in Scene Five. He moves cautiously, mysteriously. He comes to a point opposite the door; tiptoes softly up to it, listens, is impressed by the silence within, knocks carefully, as if he were guessing at the password to some secret rite. Listens. No answer. Knocks again a bit louder. No answer. Knocks impatiently, much louder.
Naw, not yet. Dat’s what I come for﻿—to join.
Naw. Dey’re all dead to de woild.
Well, you can help to wake ’em. What’s your name? I’ll make out your card.
Sure; but I been just Yank for so long﻿—Bob, dat’s it﻿—Bob Smith.
Fills out the rest of card.
But he still stands, embarrassed and uneasy.
Naw. I tought it was locked﻿—and dat yuh’d wanter give me the once-over trou a peephole or somep’n to see if I was right.
Alert and suspicious but with an easy laugh.
With a knowing grin, convinced that this is all camouflage, a part of the secrecy.
You seem to be wise to a lot of stuff none of us knows about.
Then made a bit resentful by the suspicious glances from all sides.
Aw, I know all about it.
What’d you think this is﻿—the Elks﻿—or the Black Hand?
De Elks, hell! De Black Hand, dey’re a lot of yellow backstickin’ Ginees. Naw. Dis is a man’s gang, ain’t it?
You said it! That’s why we stand on our two feet in the open. We got no secrets.
Den yuh sure got your noive wit youse!
Yuh call me? Well, I got noive, too! Here’s my hand. Yuh wanter blow tings up, don’t yuh? Well, dat’s me! I belong!
Dynamite! Blow it offen de oith﻿—steel﻿—all de cages﻿—all de factories, steamers, buildings, jails﻿—de Steel Trust and all dat makes it go.
President of the Steel Trust, you mean? Do you want to assassinate him?
Eagerly, with a touch of bravado.
No gat, no knife. Shall we give him what’s what and put the boots to him?
Aroused by the word to fierce but futile struggles.
He turns a bitter mocking face up like an ape gibbering at the moon.
Who has come up the street in time to hear this last﻿—with grim humor.
Looking up at him﻿—with a hard, bitter laugh.
Enuf to gimme life for! I was born, see? Sure, dat’s de charge. Write it in de blotter. I was born, get me!
Giving him a push﻿—with a grin, indifferently.

Twilight of the next day. The monkey house at the Zoo. One spot of clear gray light falls on the front of one cage so that the interior can be seen. The other cages are vague, shrouded in shadow from which chatterings pitched in a conversational tone can be heard. On the one cage a sign from which the word “gorilla” stands out. The gigantic animal himself is seen squatting on his haunches on a bench in much the same attitude as Rodin’s Thinker. Yank enters from the left. Immediately a chorus of angry chattering and screeching breaks out. The gorilla turns his eyes but makes no sound or move.
He laughs﻿—then in a savage tone.
He grabs hold of the bars of the cage and hauls himself painfully to his feet﻿—looks around him bewilderedly﻿—forces a mocking laugh.
In the strident tones of a circus barker.
He slips in a heap on the floor and dies. The monkeys set up a chattering, whimpering wail. And, perhaps, the Hairy Ape at last belongs.
